The Conference Board's consumer confidence index jumped 11.4 points in November to 103.3, the highest since January 2025, topping every estimate in Bloomberg's survey. The 11.4-point rise was the biggest since May 2025, per ZeroHedge, and a second straight beat of more than 10 points.

▪ Present Situation: 132.8 (+13.7), the highest since July 2025, per Bloomberg.

▪ Four of five components improved; only expected income eased.
▪ Jobs "plentiful": 30.8%, the highest of 2026. "Hard to get": 18.4%, the lowest of 2026. The gap (+12.4) is the widest of the year and more than four times July's low.
▪ Expected jobs: net −1.2%, from −10.4%, the least pessimistic reading of the year.
▪ Expected business conditions turned positive (+2.3%) for the first time this year.
▪ Average 12-month inflation expectations: 5.7%, down for a second month.
▪ More consumers said a recession is "not likely."
▪ Plans to buy autos, homes and durable goods all improved, and vacation plans rose to 44.9%.
▪ Confidence rose in every age group, led by Gen Z. Democrats and Independents "improved sharply," while Republicans "fell slightly."

As I mentioned in the first post, the Dallas Fed's modeling assumes diesel prices stay steady, but @C_Barraud's Morning Brief had evidence that diesel prices will be notably lower than the Dallas Fed's scenarios assume. That would mean fuel's boost to core PCE unwinds sooner and by more.

In particular, @JKempEnergy noted that fund managers are now more bearish on diesel and other middle distillates than at any point since the US-Iran conflict began in late February. They're betting record refinery output will keep easing what had been an extreme diesel shortage.

▪️ As of Nov. 17, hedge funds and other money managers held a combined net long of 42M barrels in U.S. diesel and European gasoil (35th percentile of all weeks since 2011). That's less than half the 88M (76th percentile) they held at the start of September. U.S. diesel alone is down to just 4M (33rd percentile), vs. 80M (83rd percentile) in gasoline.
▪️With elevated diesel margins, refiners have been processing crude at unprecedented rates into late autumn. U.S. distillate stocks rose 6M barrels from Oct. 30 to Nov. 13, the fastest for that time of year in more than 20 years, when that stretch usually brings a draw of about 3M.
▪️ Wholesale prices are already moving. Front-month U.S. diesel futures have averaged almost $29/bbl less so far in November than in September, vs. an $8 drop in crude. In inflation-adjusted terms, diesel's premium over crude fell from a record $109/bbl in September to $88 in November.
▪️ At the pump, both fuels are already below the mid-October levels the Dallas Fed's "no change" scenario holds flat. As of Nov. 16, retail diesel was down 4.7% to $5.94 and gasoline down 11.7% to $3.81, per the EIA.

@C_Barraud's Morning Brief has a @MikeZaccardi post on a new Dallas Fed study estimating that higher fuel prices added 0.2–0.6 percentage points to 12-month core PCE inflation as of September, with the effect expected to fade through 2027.

That 0.2–0.6 pt range is the spread across three different methods the authors used to estimate how much fuel prices pass through to core inflation. Each one uses the same fuel prices (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and natural gas).

Here are more details:

▪️ The models: a statistical model of how fuel-price shocks feed through to inflation (a "VAR," 0.17 pt); an approach that estimates the effect on each of 149 individual PCE components and adds them up (0.49 pt); and one that estimates it on core PCE as a whole (0.57 pt).
▪️ They disagree on exactly how big the effect is, but all three say the fuel contribution has risen 0.35–0.37 pt since September 2025. Over that same span, core PCE rose 0.30 pt (from 2.82% to 3.12%).
▪️ So on every estimate, core PCE with the fuel effect taken out is no higher than a year ago (2.55–2.95% vs. 2.62–2.99%). It's also down 0.07–0.11 pt since February, before the Iran strikes.
▪️ The size of the effect isn't unprecedented. The core-PCE-as-a-whole measure peaked at 0.63 pt in May, the highest since May 2023 (the high in data back to 2010 is 0.82 pt in March 2023). The component-by-component measure's 0.55 pt in May was the highest since August 2022.
▪️ Diesel, the fuel of the freight economy, is where the pressure has been. Retail diesel hit a record $6.53/gal on Sept. 22, up about 70% from late February, vs. about 50% for gasoline, while natural gas has barely moved.

In the Dallas Fed's "no change" scenario (fuel holding at mid-October levels), the fuel contribution stays around 0.57–0.60 pt through January. That means the core PCE prints for October through January still carry the full fuel boost. It only drops sharply from March to May, as the war-driven increases fall out of the 12-month comparison. It bottoms at 0.15 pt in September 2027, a 0.42 pt drag from today, before bouncing to 0.24 pt by December (the study's "roughly 30 basis points" decline). But that "no change" scenario is already out of date: retail diesel rose to $6.35 in late October, then fell for three straight weeks to below $6 by mid-November, per EIA data.

So while Fed members have been insistent on a broadening of price pressures, according to this study at least, the past year's acceleration in core PCE came from fuel.

The usual caveats apply. The authors say these estimates are imprecise and assume historical relationships still hold. The VAR model also leaves core without the fuel effect near 3%, still well above the Fed's 2% target, so on that estimate underlying inflation is still too high even if it isn't accelerating.

Still, the direction is the same on every model, and the fuel boost is set to reverse just as the Fed may be completing an accelerated hiking cycle.

Since 1990, the VIX has fallen 25% or more in a day only six other times: June 2006, April 2017, May 2010, August 2011, August 2024 and April 2025. The S&P 500 was higher six and 12 months later every time, with median gains of 13.8% and 20.7% (vs. 5.7% and 11.9% for all days). 

The near term was more of a coin flip, though. It was higher a week later in three of the six and a month later in four (median +1.1%), and in three of the six it fell more than 5% further within three months.

Loosening to drops of 20% or more (22 prior cases), the S&P 500 was higher a month later 82% of the time (median +2.0%), vs. 64% for all days. 

When the drop came from a VIX of 30 or higher, as Monday’s did, the record is more mixed: the S&P 500 was lower three months later in four of nine cases, all between 2007 and 2010.

One of the charts in last night's @DailyChartbook nightly email was from Carson's great @RyanDetrick, noting that "faster 10% corrections historically haven't been as likely to fall into a bear market." Since 1928, those that hit −10% within 20 trading days of a record became bear markets 3 of 9 times, vs. 9 of 17 slower ones.

I dug into the data, and fast corrections haven't just been less likely to turn into bears. They've also tended to bounce back faster.

This one took 33 trading days to reach −10% (October 6 record to Friday's close). Looking at corrections that got there in 33 days or fewer since 1928:

▪️ 4 of 11 (36%) became bear markets, vs. 8 of 15 (53%) for slower ones.
▪️ The bottom came a median of just 17 trading days after the first −10% close, vs. 112 for slower corrections.
▪️ The S&P's median return from that first −10% close was +16.8% over the next 6 months (9 of 11 higher), vs. +3.0% for slower corrections and +4.9% for all days since 1928.
▪️ 12 months out, the median gain was +17.6% (8 of 11 higher), vs. +7.0%.
▪️ They got back to a new record in a median of 126 trading days, vs. 375 for slower corrections.

The exceptions were 1929 and 2007, two not great years, so it's not a guarantee. But history says the speed of this pullback is more a feature than a bug, and Monday's +4.7% rally is a decent start.

That 0.2–0.6 pt range is the spread across three different methods the authors used to estimate how much fuel prices pass through to core inflation. Each one uses the same fuel prices (gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and natural gas).

Here are more details:

▪️ The models: a statistical model of how fuel-price shocks feed through to inflation (a "VAR," 0.17 pt); an approach that estimates the effect on each of 149 individual PCE components and adds them up (0.49 pt); and one that estimates it on core PCE as a whole (0.57 pt).
▪️ They disagree on exactly how big the effect is, but all three say the fuel contribution has risen 0.35–0.37 pt since September 2025. Over that same span, core PCE rose 0.30 pt (from 2.82% to 3.12%).
▪️ So on every estimate, core PCE with the fuel effect taken out is no higher than a year ago (2.55–2.95% vs. 2.62–2.99%). It's also down 0.07–0.11 pt since February, before the Iran strikes.
▪️ The size of the effect isn't unprecedented. The core-PCE-as-a-whole measure peaked at 0.63 pt in May, the highest since May 2023 (the high in data back to 2010 is 0.82 pt in March 2023). The component-by-component measure's 0.55 pt in May was the highest since August 2022.
▪️ Diesel, the fuel of the freight economy, is where the pressure has been. Retail diesel hit a record $6.53/gal on Sept. 22, up about 70% from late February, vs. about 50% for gasoline, while natural gas has barely moved.

In the Dallas Fed's "no change" scenario (fuel holding at mid-October levels), the fuel contribution stays around 0.57–0.60 pt through January. That means the core PCE prints for October through January still carry the full fuel boost. It only drops sharply from March to May, as the war-driven increases fall out of the 12-month comparison. It bottoms at 0.15 pt in September 2027, a 0.42 pt drag from today, before bouncing to 0.24 pt by December (the study's "roughly 30 basis points" decline). But that "no change" scenario is already out of date: retail diesel rose to $6.35 in late October, then fell for three straight weeks to below $6 by mid-November, per EIA data.

So while Fed members have been insistent on a broadening of price pressures, according to this study at least, the past year's acceleration in core PCE came from fuel.

The usual caveats apply. The authors say these estimates are imprecise and assume historical relationships still hold. The VAR model also leaves core without the fuel effect near 3%, still well above the Fed's 2% target, so on that estimate underlying inflation is still too high even if it isn't accelerating.

Still, the direction is the same on every model, and the fuel boost is set to reverse just as the Fed may be completing an accelerated hiking cycle.

Christophe Barraud's (@C_Barraud) Monday Morning Brief flagged Korea's early November trade data, and it shows no letup in the AI chip boom, even as Korean chip stocks have been cut in half.

Per the Korea Customs Service, exports in the first 20 days of November:

▪️ Rose 101.5% y/y to $77.4B, the most for the first 20 days of any month (the prior high was $71.4B in September).
▪️ Adjusted for working days (16 vs 15.5), the daily average rose 95.2% to $4.84B, also a record for any 1–20 stretch, topping October's $4.74B.
▪️ Chip exports jumped 294.4% to a record $38.5B, 49.7% of the total (up 24.3 points from a year ago). By my math, chips supplied ~74% of the $39B y/y gain.
▪️ It isn't only chips though. Computer peripherals rose 330.5% and petroleum products 91.9% (mostly oil prices), while autos fell 5.6%. Non-chip exports were up ~36%.
▪️ Year-to-date exports reached ~$1.008T through November 20, up 63.2%.

The disconnect with markets is striking:

▪️ The KOSPI closed Monday at 4,708.54, its lowest since January 13 and 48.3% below its June 22 record (9,114.55).
▪️ SK hynix is ~63% off its 2026 high and Samsung ~51%.
▪️ Friday's 5.2% drop came on a worsening outlook for chip prices and tighter US curbs on China's access to chips.

So much of the export surge is price rather than volume that Korea's 10- and 20-day releases are one of the fastest and most high-frequency checks on how that is holding up. So far the data say very well: first-20-day chip exports have climbed from $25.5B in June to $38.5B in November. The next checks are the full November figures on December 1 and the December 1–10 data around December 11.

After a set of weak Treasury auctions two weeks ago, Monday's two-year was much improved across the board:

Monday’s $69 billion 2-year auction stopped through (yield below expectations) after the 30-year, 10-year and 3-year all tailed two weeks ago. Bid-to-cover rose, dealers took less, and indirect bidders (which include foreign buyers) bounced from October’s lowest share since 2021.

▪️ Stop-through: 0.3 basis point (4.700% high yield vs. 4.703% when-issued), first since August, vs. a 0.3 basis point tail in October and a 0.1 basis point stop-through six-month average.

▪️ Bid-to-cover: 2.65, highest since July, vs. 2.59 in October and a 2.63 six-month average.

▪️ Dealers: 10.4%, lowest since July, vs. 13.0% in October and an 11.5% six-month average.

▪️ Indirect: 51.5% vs. 45.7% in October (lowest since November 2021) although still down from a 56.5% six-month average.

▪️ Direct: 38.1%, third-highest since bidder data began in 2008, vs. a record 41.3% in October and a 32.0% six-month average.

▪️ High yield: 4.700% vs. 4.708% in October and a 4.379% six-month average.

@investingLive_’s Greg Michalowski graded it a B−. ZeroHedge called it “a solid, if generally average, auction.”

A stop-through with a higher bid-to-cover and less left to dealers is a welcome change. The indirect share was still though below its six-month average.  Tuesday’s 5-year and Wednesday’s 7-year will give us more color on demand further up the curve.

So what happens after opens like this?  Outside of the Tech bust, it's been a long-term buying opportunity but more mixed short-term for the Nasdaq.

I looked at every S&P 500 open at least 2% above the prior close and every Nasdaq open at least 3% above (about 3 standard deviations each) since 2000. I counted only the first in any one-month cluster and measured from the close of the gap day.

Short term, the S&P has usually kept going. The Nasdaq has been choppier:

▪️ S&P 500 (32 cases): a week later it was higher 66% of the time (median +1.3%), and a month later 72% of the time (median +2.9%). For all days since 2000, those figures are 57% and 63% (median +0.3% and +1.2%).
▪️ Nasdaq since 2003 (11 cases): a week and a month later it was higher only 55% of the time (median +0.3% for both), below an average day. That includes one-month drops of 22% (September 2008), 9% (May 2010) and 7% (October 2008).

Longer term, both have done well:

▪️ S&P 500: median +9.5% six months later and +16.5% a year later, vs. +5.4% and +11.1% for all days.
▪️ Nasdaq since 2003: higher six months later in 10 of 11, with a median gain of +21.7% vs. +8.3% for all days.

The exception on the latter is the dot-com bust. Ten of the 21 Nasdaq cases since 2000 came in 2000–2002, when big gap-ups were mostly bear-market rallies that faded. Include them and the Nasdaq was higher a year later only 48% of the time.

Opens this big happen in stressed markets. Going into Monday, the Nasdaq was about 10% below its 200-day moving average, and 28 of the 32 S&P cases also came below that line. Outside 2000–2002, though, they've more often marked a low forming than a trap. The samples are small and 2020 and 2025 do a lot of the work, so keep that in mind.
